summary: GitHub Next is a team of approximately 20 researchers, senior developers, and tool builders who report directly to GitHub's CEO and work outside the regular product organization. Their charter is to explore the future of software engineering through a pipeline of functional prototypes, internal dogfooding, company-wide dogfooding, tech previews, and eventual productization, with kill/shelve decisions at any stage. Copilot itself originated as a Next experiment. Other experiments include Copilot for CLI, Copilot Voice, GitHub Blocks, and Speckle Lang. Pandita uses Andrew Ng's analogy of AI as the new electricity, drawing a parallel to manufacturing electrification: electric motors existed in the 1880s but took roughly 40 years to become mainstream. The first exploration, Copilot Next Edit Suggestions (NES), asks whether ghost text could be more intelligent. While Copilot excels at creating new code, developers almost always edit existing code at multiple locations. NES suggests edits beyond the current cursor. Open challenges include suggestion modality, viewport visibility, unopened files, and model fine-tuning. NES is expected as a tech preview within months. The second exploration, Copilot Workspace, moves from code completions to task completions. User feedback revealed pain points: difficulty getting started, distrust of AI output, desire to retain problem-solving, wanting AI as a thought partner, and maintaining developer control. Copilot Workspace offers one-click task proposals, a built-in runtime, an iteration environment, and collaboration via pull requests or sharing. A live demo adds a Rust example to the Monospace font playground website, showing specification generation (current and target states), plan generation identifying files to update, implementation, iterative editing via chat, an integrated terminal accepting natural language commands (especially useful on mobile), and a live preview confirming the Rust example appears. Pandita notes caching was used for demo speed but actual generation takes minutes. Future explorations include rethinking developer learning with AI and how code review changes when AI writes most code. Pandita closes by emphasizing that exploration is the path to the AI future, hoping to avoid waiting 40 years as electrification did.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: GitHub Next Introduction
sections.summary: Pandita introduces GitHub Next as a team of about 20 researchers, senior developers, and tool builders who report directly to the CEO and work outside the regular product organization, exploring the future of software engineering and passing learnings to product teams.

sections.title: AI as the New Electricity and Exploration Process
sections.summary: Draws analogy between AI and electricity using Andrew Ng's quote and the history of manufacturing electrification from the 1880s to 1920s, explaining that transformative technology requires extended exploration. Describes GitHub Next's dogfooding pipeline from prototype to product, noting Copilot originated as a Next experiment.

sections.title: Copilot Next Edit Suggestions
sections.summary: Introduces Next Edit Suggestions, motivated by making ghost text more intelligent. While Copilot excels at new code creation, developers mostly edit existing code at multiple locations. NES suggests edits beyond the current cursor. Includes a Python demo showing cascading suggestions for method definition, arguments, and documentation updates.

sections.title: Next Edit Suggestions Open Challenges
sections.summary: Discusses unresolved challenges: optimal suggestion modality, handling edits outside the viewport or in unopened files, and fine-tuning models for accuracy. NES is expected to emerge as a tech preview within months.

sections.title: From Code Completions to Task Completions
sections.summary: Explains the software development inner loop (task, specification, plan, implementation) and the motivation for Copilot Workspace. Describes how separate explorations in natural language specification and runtime-informed code completions merged into Copilot Workspace.

sections.title: User Feedback and Copilot Workspace Features
sections.summary: User feedback revealed pain points: difficulty getting started, distrust of AI output, desire to retain problem-solving, wanting AI as a thought partner, and maintaining developer control. Copilot Workspace offers one-click proposals, built-in runtime, iteration environment, and collaboration via pull requests or workspace sharing.

sections.title: Copilot Workspace Demo: Adding Rust to Monospace Playground
sections.summary: Live demo begins with the Monospace font playground website. An issue requests adding a Rust syntax highlighting example. Copilot Workspace generates current and target specifications, a plan identifying three files to update, and an implementation. Caching is used for demo speed; actual generation takes minutes. Users can iteratively edit plans and code via chat at any point.

sections.title: Copilot Workspace Demo: Terminal, Preview, and Mobile
sections.summary: Demo continues with an integrated terminal accepting natural language commands to install and run the repo. A live preview confirms the Rust example renders correctly. Pandita highlights that natural language terminal commands are especially useful on mobile devices where typing symbols is tedious.

sections.title: Future Explorations and Closing
sections.summary: Pandita mentions future explorations including rethinking developer learning with AI and how code review changes when AI writes most code. Some explorations will become tech previews, some will be killed. He closes by reiterating that exploration is the path to the AI future, hoping to avoid the 40-year wait experienced with electrification, and invites attendees to live demos at the Microsoft booth.
